stemMd: In the last paragraph the narrator looks at the tide clock and finds "that I already knew what they would say." This statement most strongly suggests that the narrator has:

options.label: A
options.textMd: concluded that the tide clock and the clock on the stove had been showing the same hour all along.

options.label: B
options.textMd: discovered that the clock really had been broken and that Nan had quietly repaired it that summer.

options.label: C
options.textMd: memorised the fixed departure times that Nan finally agreed to send to the mainland bus company.

options.label: D
options.textMd: learned to read the tide in the water itself, so the clock merely confirms what the narrator sees.

explanationMd:
Track what changes across the passage. At the start, the narrator can see the water but says plainly, "I could see the water; I could not see the hour in it" — the clock is unreadable because the tide itself is unreadable. The turning point is the August evening: after watching the flats for an hour and a half, the narrator finally sees slack water and hears Nan name it.

Only then does the narrator go inside and find the clock's two hands already intelligible. Nothing about the clock has changed; what has changed is the narrator's ability to read the tide. That is exactly what the choice saying the narrator has learned to read the tide in the water itself, so that the clock merely confirms it, says.

To check the answer, ask what the sentence would have to mean for each of the other choices to be true — a memorised timetable, a repair, or a claim that the two clocks agree — and look for a line in the passage that supports it. There is none: the passage says the schedule was never printed and changed every day and that Nan twice refused the bus company fixed times, never says the clock was repaired, and states that the tide clock "never agreed with the clock on the stove."

distractorRationale.c: Assumes there were fixed departure times to memorise and that Nan gave way to the bus company. The second paragraph says the opposite: the schedule was never printed "because it changed every day," and Nan twice refused the company's request for fixed times, writing back that "the sea did not take instruction."
distractorRationale.b: Takes the child's early belief that the clock was "broken" as the passage's actual position. That belief is presented as a misunderstanding the narrator held "for the first eleven summers," and nothing in the passage describes Nan or anyone else repairing the clock.
distractorRationale.a: Contradicts the first paragraph, which states that the tide clock "never agreed with the clock on the stove." The point of the ending is that the narrator can now read a different measure, not that the two clocks turned out to show the same hour.

accessibilityText: The question asks what the narrator means by the final sentence of the passage, in which the narrator looks at the two hands of the numberless tide clock and finds that the narrator already knew what they would say.

independentSolve.workingNotes: The narrator has just watched the flats long enough to see slack water with her own eyes, then goes inside and finds she already knows what the tide clock says, so she has learned to read the tide from the water and the clock only confirms it. The two clocks 'never agreed', so the same-hour option contradicts the text; nothing says the clock was repaired or that Nan ever sent fixed times to the bus company. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-cue-batch1-run1) reached the same answer: The narrator has just watched the water and seen slack water for the first time. Going inside, they find they already know what the tide clock says, so they now read the tide from the water and the clock only confirms it. The 'same hour as the stove clock' option contradicts the opening, where the two clocks never agree. The passage never says the clock was repaired or that fixed times were sent, so those two options have no support.]
